findings.title: New abstract getShortcut() breaks custom grant-type factories
findings.body: OAuth2GrantTypeFactory is an extension interface, but getShortcut() was added as an abstract method without a default implementation. Existing custom grant factories compiled against the old interface will fail with AbstractMethodError when DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit() iterates all OAuth2GrantType factories and calls getShortcut(), and source implementations will no longer compile. This can break server startup or token issuance for deployments with custom grants. Provide a default implementation, for example returning the unknown shortcut, so existing factories continue to work.

findings.title: Public OAuth2GrantType.Context copy constructor was removed
findings.body: The previously public Context(Context) copy constructor has been removed while changing the main constructor to derive grantType from formParams. Code in custom grant types or delegating/wrapping grant implementations that used new OAuth2GrantType.Context(existingContext) will now fail to compile, and already-compiled code will fail with NoSuchMethodError. The copy constructor should be retained, copying grantType as well, or at least deprecated through a compatibility cycle.

findings.title: Unknown grant type now fails all access-token issuance instead of falling back
findings.body: TokenManager.initToken() calls encodeTokenId() for every access token, and encodeTokenId() throws IllegalStateException when the GRANT_TYPE client-session attribute is a non-null value that is not exactly a registered OAuth2GrantTypeFactory id. Token creation previously succeeded in that situation, and getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext() already treats a missing grant as the unknown value 'na'; an unregistered, aliased, or extension-supplied grant string now turns token issuance into a server error instead of using the same unknown fallback.

findings.title: Grant shortcut length is documented inconsistently and never validated
findings.body: OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut() javadoc describes the value as 'usually like 3-letters', but DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider encodes session, token and grant shortcuts without validating length and getTokenContextFromTokenId() requires the whole encoded prefix to be exactly 6 characters, i.e. exactly 2 characters per shortcut. A factory following the javadoc and returning a 3-letter shortcut, or returning a 1-letter/empty/null shortcut, produces token IDs that the decoder rejects, or fails with an NPE from the ConcurrentHashMap, instead of being rejected clearly at startup. Document exactly two characters and validate uniqueness and length in postInit() and in the lazy refresh paths.

findings.title: Decoding throws on malformed or newer token IDs instead of returning UNKNOWN
findings.body: getTokenContextFromTokenId() returns UNKNOWN for legacy token IDs without a colon, but throws IllegalArgumentException for any colon-containing ID whose prefix is not exactly 6 characters or whose session/token/grant shortcut is unknown to this node. That is inconsistent backward-compatibility handling: during rolling upgrades, or when the planned introspection/userinfo consumers decode tokens issued by a newer node with a new shortcut, validation would fail with an exception rather than falling back to the normal session lookup. Unknown or malformed encodings should be treated like legacy IDs and return UNKNOWN context.

findings.title: isAccessTokenId matcher checks the wrong substring and inverts the comparison
findings.body: The encoded token ID format is two chars session type, two chars token type, then two chars grant type, so the grant shortcut is items[0].substring(4, 6). The matcher uses substring(3, 5) and returns false when that substring equals expectedGrantShortcut. For a normal ID such as onrtac the checked substring is 'ta', never 'ac', so expectCodeToToken, expectRefresh, expectDeviceCodeToToken and expectAuthReqIdToToken pass regardless of the encoded grant type as long as the raw part is a UUID; the new grant-encoding behaviour is effectively untested by these integration assertions.

findings.title: Constructor validates grantType twice and never validates rawTokenId
findings.body: The fourth constructor check is Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed"), repeating the grantType check instead of checking the rawTokenId parameter. A null rawTokenId therefore slips through and encodeTokenId() silently produces an ID ending in ':null', which later decodes to the literal raw ID "null" rather than failing fast at construction.
